newsitem.title: THAILAND: Markets to remain cool to Thai bank shares.
newsitem.headline: Markets to remain cool to Thai bank shares.

text.p: Respectable profits and more conservative lending practices are unlikely to reverse negative sentiment towards badly mauled bank and finance stocks in the fragile Thai bourse, analysts said on Monday.

Heavy selling of Thai blue-chip banks and finance counters by foreign institutional investors since early October have pushed the stock market to its lowest level in more than three years, according to brokers.
Since the start of October, the banking sector has declined 18.9 percent and finance and securities 27.5 percent. Share prices are still falling.

Analysts said even reports of encouraging third-quarter earnings expected for financial institutions would not allay market concerns over Thailand's poor economic fundamentals and political uncertainty ahead of a general election on November 17.

Bank profits, which account for almost half of all profits made by Thai listed companies, are widely expected to increase by 8 to 10 percent over the year, below the 15 to 18 percent improvement forecast at the start of the year.

"I just don't think any numbers (results) will make a change in this market. No one really cares about results at the moment," said a senior bank analyst. "The thing right now is the amount of money the institutions have in this market...Most other markets in Asia and Latin America are perceived as a better buy on political stability."

Thailand's economic growth is seen by many analysts slowing to around 6.8 percent this year, down from 8.6 percent last year, in part due to a slump in export growth to 5.5 percent in the first eight months of this year from 26 percent in 1995, they added.
With 70 percent of domestic borrowing coming through the Thai commercial banks, analysts said bank prospects were intrinsically linked to overall economic improvement.

"Thai banks are much stronger now, in terms of balance sheets, than at any time in the last two years," said Thanawat Patchimkul, banking analyst at Seamico Securities Plc. "But with the economic downturn the problems must be seen as greater than in the past.
"While everything is looking cheap at the moment we are expecting some more bad news over the next few months and don't see much of an improvement until this time next year."

Bank funding costs have risen after Moody's Investor Service downgraded the country's short-term sovereign debt from Prime-1 to Prime-2. Recent central bank curbs on overseas borrowing also have added to the cost of funds.
Some analysts said foreign banks were becoming cautious in lending to Thai banks.

Researchers said annual loan growth, capped by the central bank at 21 percent, was not likely to exceed 10-11 percent this year as the leading banks adopt more conservative lending practices in the weaker economic environment.

Siam Commercial Bank's preliminary figures showing 17 percent growth in year-on-year third-quarter profits has not affected market sentiment. Neither has Siam City Bank's figures showing a 56 percent increase in profits.

"I think everyone knows the market is on a downturn," said an analyst at Nithipat Capital Plc. "Cheaper valuations are not seen as a good enough reason for investors to come in. I think there needs to be more transparency of debt provisioning which may start to happen over the next year."
Concerns surrounding loan quality are even more acute in the finance and securities sector, where lending to the flagging Thai property sector is heavy.
